bibliography.abstract: Reducing the number of vehicle through lanes and dedicating the space to other purposes like parking, multimodal infrastructure, or turning lanes (i.e., road diets) has become more popular due to its cost-effectiveness as a strategy to increase multimodal accessibility and safety for all road users. However, methodological challenges and data gaps make it difficult to quickly assess opportunities for statewide implementation. A data-driven framework for evaluating the feasibility and opportunity of road diets throughout Louisiana is presented in this study. A replicable method is created for assessing more than 1.8 million 0.1-mile roadway segments by combining state agency’s design guidelines with roadway geometry, traffic operations, land use, human activities, crash data, and speed data. Traffic thresholds, design standards, and geometric compliance were used to evaluate feasibility. Results show that 1.8% (3091 miles) of the road segments are feasible for lane width adjustment, and 0.5% (569 miles) for lane reduction. Opportunity measures were developed from mobility analytics (to reflect active transportation demand), spatial relationships with nearby businesses (to reflect parking needs), historical crash and speeding data analysis (to reflect safety improvement potential). Among feasible segments, opportunity priority is assigned based on the calculated active transportation investment score, parking need score, road diet-related crash rate, and speeding rate. A case study is included to illustrate the effectiveness of the framework. The suggested approach offers flexibility for adaptation to local context while improving consistency and transparency in statewide screening programs. This study demonstrates how investments that enhance roadway function and community outcomes can be more targeted by combining traditional design evaluation with cutting-edge data sources.
bibliography.title: Expanding feasibility and opportunity measures with emerging datasets for statewide road diet screening in Louisiana

en.what: The authors developed a data-driven screening framework to evaluate road diet potential across 1.8 million 0.1-mile roadway segments in Louisiana by combining state design guidelines with geometric, operational, land use, crash, speed, and mobility data. The screening found that 1.8% (3,091 miles) of evaluated road segments are candidate sites for lane width adjustments, while 0.5% (569 miles) are suitable for complete lane reductions. Feasible segments were subsequently prioritized using composite scores reflecting active transportation demand, parking needs, safety history, and speeding rates.
en.why: The framework establishes a consistent, transparent method for state agencies to rapidly screen entire road networks for reallocation opportunities rather than relying on site-by-site evaluations.
